newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Mother's Day bouquets may be 'stained with blood'.
newsitem.headline: Mother's Day bouquets may be 'stained with blood'.

text.p: International labour unions said Friday that labour and environmental abuses were widespread in the rapidly expanding global flower industry and warned that Mother's Day bouquets could be "stained with blood."

"Are Mother's Day flowers stained with blood?" the International Union of Food and Agricultural Workers asked in a summary of a study it commissioned to look into the international flower industry, in which developing countries are increasingly taking over production .

The IUF presented a video that it said showed that "hazardous conditions for workers and the pollution of the environment through the reckless application of toxic chemicals are the consequences of denying workers elementary trade union and democratic rights."

It showed workers blinded by toxic sprays and women who had miscarried or given birth prematurely after working in flower greenhouses. Industry employees were often paid less per day than the price of one flower sold in Europe, it said.

Although it focused on Colombia and Uganda, two of the main suppliers to the world market, the study found clandestine workers in the Dutch flower industry -- under fire for extensive use of pesticides -- were vulnerable to abuse.

The investigation was sponsored by the IUF, the Geneva-based International Federaton of Commercial Employees, the Brussels-based International Confederation of Free Trade Unions and the Dutch trade union centre FNV.

In the video, the IUF said, women in Colombia and Uganda describe being forced to work close to chemical spraying in greenhouses -- which are often built on former farm land, depriving local populations of food resources.

The report said developing countries now held over 25 percent of the world trade in flowers -- which is heavily reliant on the airline industry for quick delivery to the major markets in the United States, Europe and Japan.
The EU, it said, was the leading importer of flowers, over 21 percent of which -- to a value of $519 million in 1995 -- came from poorer countries, mainly in Latin America and Africa.

The report said that while the flower trade in Europe had launched various forms of "eco labelling" to meet growing environmental awareness among consumers, some of these did not even conform to minimum international labour standards.

In Latin America in particular, the IUF said, workers who organised to fight for better conditions were harassed and often murdered. Colombian workers in the video masked their faces to avoid recognition by their employers.
In Uganda, it added, new foreign investors -- many encouraged by tax-shelter schemes -- denied recognition to labour unions in many sectors, including agriculture.

The video and the report, IUF General Secretary Ron Oswald said, "make it abundantly clear that only when trade union rights are respected can consumers be assured they are purchasing flowers (grown in conditions) which do not destroy the environment and threaten the health and safety of workers and their families."
